x.A: Databases on EC2 mean managing the operating system, patching, and backups, so operational overhead isn't reduced.
x.B: RDS for SQL Server is a managed database that handles patching and backups, Multi-AZ gives high availability, and KMS encryption protects the sensitive data. It increases security and reduces operational overhead.
x.C: S3 isn't a relational database, so the data model would need to change, and Macie only discovers sensitive data.
x.D: DynamoDB isn't relational, so it would need a rewrite, and CloudWatch Logs isn't a data security solution.

x.A: An Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an ALB provides high availability, and AWS WAF can be associated with the ALB to filter web requests.
x.B: A placement group isn't about availability, and WAF can't be connected to a placement group.
x.C: Two fixed instances don't scale or replace themselves, so availability and scalability are lower than with Auto Scaling.
x.D: WAF can't be connected to an Auto Scaling group, because it attaches to the ALB.

x.A: S3 access points with their own policies let each application be limited to its prefix with fine-grained control, and they're managed without editing one large bucket policy. It needs the least overhead.
x.B: A Batch Operations job to set ACLs on each object is a lot of work and ACLs are hard to manage for millions of objects.
x.C: Replicating objects into separate buckets duplicates data and increases cost and management.
x.D: Replicating into new buckets still duplicates data, and access points aren't needed once each app has its own bucket.

x.A: S3 Event Notifications to an SQS queue trigger a Lambda function as each image is uploaded. Processing takes 2 minutes and 512 MB, which fits Lambda, and you pay only for the runs, so it's the most cost-effective.
x.B: An EC2 Reserved Instance bills all the time, even when there are few uploads.
x.C: An ECS container instance runs continuously and costs more for around 150 photos a day.
x.D: An Elastic Beanstalk application runs servers all the time, which costs more.

x.A: Global Accelerator supports TCP and UDP and routes traffic to the closest healthy endpoint, which improves availability and performance for both workloads, including endpoints for the on-premises workload.
x.B: CloudFront doesn't support TCP and UDP application traffic like this and can't front on-premises UDP workloads.
x.C: ALBs support only HTTP and HTTPS, so they can't handle the stateful TCP and stateless UDP traffic.
x.D: NLBs support TCP and UDP. One NLB for the EC2 endpoints and another for on-premises endpoints give Global Accelerator targets in each Region.
x.E: An ALB can't carry UDP to the on-premises endpoints.

x.A: Denying snapshot deletion in the IAM policy would stop the cleanup script from working at all, so expired snapshots would never be deleted.
x.B: Copying snapshots to another Region adds cost, and the script could delete those too.
x.C: A Recycle Bin retention rule keeps deleted snapshots for 7 days so they can be recovered, so expired snapshots are still cleaned up eventually without keeping them indefinitely. It takes very little development.
x.D: Snapshots can't just be copied to S3 Standard-IA like that, and it needs custom work.

x.A: A gateway VPC endpoint is for resources inside a VPC, and CloudFormation (a service) doesn't use your VPC endpoint to fetch the template.
x.B: An API Gateway REST API in front of S3 means building and securing an API just for a template, which is more work.
x.C: A presigned URL gives CloudFormation temporary access to the template in the private bucket for the specific request, with no public access and no extra infrastructure.
x.D: Making the template public even briefly exposes it and goes against security best practices.

x.A: IAM Identity Center gives the external engineers console access with temporary credentials, and Session Manager gives OS access to instances in private subnets through IAM permissions, with no open ports, SSH keys, or bastion hosts. It's the most secure.
x.B: Local IAM user credentials in each account are long-term credentials to manage, which is less secure than IAM Identity Center.
x.C: SSH access from IP ranges, SSH key pairs, and local IAM users means open ports, key management, and long-term credentials.
x.D: A bastion host, SSH keys, and IAM users add exposed infrastructure and long-term credentials, which is less secure.

x.A: A cross-Region read replica adds replication cost and latency, and isn't needed when the reports are in the same Region.
x.B: The standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment can't serve queries, so reports can't run on it.
x.C: DMS to a new database needs a replication instance and ongoing management, which costs more.
x.D: A read replica in us-east-1 serves the near real-time reports so they don't slow the production database, and it costs less than the other options.

x.A: Sending logs to Redshift and QuickSight is a heavy analytics pipeline and doesn't give instance metrics at 2 minute granularity.
x.B: Detailed monitoring publishes EC2 metrics to CloudWatch every 1 minute, which meets a granularity of no more than 2 minutes (basic monitoring is every 5 minutes).
x.C: A Lambda function to fetch logs doesn't change the metric granularity, because logs aren't metrics.
x.D: Exporting logs to S3 and Redshift is a heavy pipeline that doesn't give performance metrics at the needed granularity.

x.A: A long-running EMR cluster is costly for around 150 photos a day.
x.B: An always-on EC2 instance polling every minute costs far more than needed.
x.C: An S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function for each new photo. Lambda generates the thumbnail, and you pay only for the few runs a day, so it's the cheapest.
x.D: S3 Storage Lens reports metrics and can't invoke Lambda for each upload.

x.A: A script on EC2 means managing a server and isn't serverless, and deleting millions of objects through the CLI is slow.
x.B: AWS Batch runs containers on compute resources, so it isn't a serverless solution for this and needs setup.
x.C: A Glue crawler isn't designed to list and filter objects for deletion, and the script means more work.
x.D: S3 Inventory lists the objects, a Lambda function filters out the data to keep and deletes the rest, and S3 Batch Operations invokes it at scale from the inventory report. It's serverless.

x.A: A shared role with full bucket access breaks least privilege, since every function could read all data.
x.B: A bucket policy based on VPC endpoint IP addresses limits network sources and can't distinguish individual functions.
x.C: An individual IAM role for each Lambda function, with only the S3 access that function needs, follows least privilege, and only the authorized functions can access the data.
x.D: Bucket policies can't grant access by Lambda function ARN, because the principal is the function's execution role.

x.A: Keeping MySQL on an EC2 Reserved Instance means managing the database, which adds operational overhead compared with RDS.
x.B: CloudFront and S3 serve the static frontend securely worldwide, Lambda with API Gateway runs the backend microservices with no servers, and RDS for MySQL is a managed database. It has the least operational overhead.
x.C: Lambda functions in a target group behind an NLB isn't valid, because NLB can't invoke Lambda.
x.D: This leaves the database on EC2 and doesn't use CloudFront, so it isn't globally available or low in overhead.

x.A: S3 with CloudFront serves static objects, so it isn't suitable for fast, near real-time rankings that change continuously.
x.B: EC2 instances in multiple Regions with Route 53 means managing servers and keeping player data consistent across Regions.
x.C: ElastiCache for Redis has sorted sets that rank players in near real time with very fast access, and it can persist data to disk, so data survives a restart. It's managed, so it needs little work.
x.D: Memcached has no persistence, so data would be lost on a restart.

x.A: Storing keys in an S3 bucket isn't secure or centralized key management and isn't KMS.
x.B: A hardware security appliance is more infrastructure to run, and you don't need it to use KMS.
x.C: One KMS key for all customers means data isn't encrypted separately per customer.
x.D: Separate KMS keys for each customer encrypt each customer's data separately, with granular access control and CloudTrail logging, and KMS is a managed, centralized solution.

x.A: A NAT gateway doesn't manage web traffic, and storing orders on Auto Scaling EC2 instances risks losing them.
x.B: Redshift is a data warehouse and isn't designed to store orders for transactions, and two load balancers are unnecessary.
x.C: A Gateway Load Balancer is for virtual appliances, and it can't capture and store orders.
x.D: An ALB manages web traffic, an Auto Scaling group handles increases in load, SQS holds unprocessed orders durably so none are lost, and RDS Multi-AZ stores the processed orders reliably.

x.A: Grouping small 10 KB files into large objects avoids per-object overhead and the minimum object size charges of Glacier classes. Glacier Instant Retrieval holds them immediately available the first year at low cost, and Deep Archive is cheapest for the 7 year archive.
x.B: Standard-IA costs more than Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely accessed data, and a transition from IA to Instant Retrieval at 1 year costs more than Deep Archive.
x.C: Millions of small 10 KB files in Glacier classes are charged at the 128 KB minimum per object, which makes it costly, and Flexible Retrieval at 7 years costs more than Deep Archive.
x.D: Standard-IA charges a 128 KB minimum per object, which makes it costly for millions of 10 KB files.

x.A: A single io1 volume is limited to 64,000 IOPS, so striping several io1 volumes with LVM adds up IOPS and throughput beyond one volume's limit, improving storage performance.
x.B: 64,000 IOPS is the maximum for an io1 volume, so you can't go higher on a single volume.
x.C: Increasing the size doesn't raise the IOPS above the limit of 64,000.
x.D: A storage optimized instance has local storage, but the data is on EBS, and the performance limit comes from the single volume.

x.A: SQS is a queue where each message is consumed by one reader, so it isn't a pub/sub pattern with multiple subscribers.
x.B: SNS is the right pub/sub service, but API Gateway REST APIs cost more per request than HTTP APIs.
x.C: Kinesis Data Streams with enhanced fan-out costs more and is for streaming data, which is more than needed.
x.D: An API Gateway HTTP API is cheaper than a REST API, Lambda publishes events to an SNS topic, and multiple subscribers receive them. It's serverless, event-driven, loosely coupled, and the most cost-effective.

x.A: A bigger instance reduces CPU utilization on the single EC2 instance, an Auto Scaling group of 1 replaces the instance if it fails, and an RDS read replica improves read performance. The design is limited to one instance, so this meets the needs.
x.B: Redirecting all read and write traffic to a read replica isn't possible because replicas are read-only.
x.C: The application can run only on a single EC2 instance, so a maximum of 2 isn't allowed, and the EC2 CPU problem isn't solved.
x.D: A larger RDS instance costs more and doesn't separate read load, so a read replica is the better fix.

x.A: Sharing IAM user credentials breaks accountability and security.
x.B: IAM roles with fine-grained permissions based on least privilege, assigned to each developer, give temporary credentials and only the access they need.
x.C: Long-lived access keys are a security risk, and the question doesn't need them.
x.D: Cognito user pools are for application users, not for giving developers access to AWS resources.

x.A: Compute Optimizer can recommend a larger instance to scale vertically, but that's a single instance that stays a single point of failure and costs more.
x.B: An AMI from the web server and a launch template let new instances be created identically, which is needed for an Auto Scaling group.
x.C: Auto Scaling and an ALB scale horizontally, not vertically.
x.D: Compute Optimizer recommends instance types for the sizes, but it doesn't scale horizontally.
x.E: An Auto Scaling group with an ALB adds instances when CPU is high, which solves the performance problem and improves availability across instances.

x.A: Network Access Analyzer reviews network access paths, not IAM user permissions.
x.B: A CloudWatch alarm on resource changes doesn't review permissions granted to users.
x.C: IAM Access Analyzer finds unused access and over-permissive policies, and can review all accounts in the organization from one place, so it needs the least overhead.
x.D: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities, not excessive IAM permissions.

x.A: Governance mode lets users with special permissions override the lock and delete or change objects, so it doesn't strictly prevent deletion or modification.
x.B: Object Lock in compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting or modifying the objects for the retention period, which meets the regulatory requirement.
x.C: Versioning with a lifecycle delete rule doesn't protect objects from being deleted before the period ends.
x.D: Moving objects to Glacier doesn't prevent deletion or modification.
